en: Clever at understanding situations and turning them to one's advantage
hook: ASTUTE: A STUDENT who sees through everything.
story: Astute. Clever at understanding situations and using them to your advantage. When a new supermarket opened next to her small grocery in Mirpur, Nasima did not panic. She noticed the big store closed at ten, so she stayed open until midnight. She learned the names of her regular customers' children and stocked the fresh fish the supermarket never had. She was astute. Astute sounds a little like a student: an astute person reads people and markets alike. So, what word describes someone who sharply understands a situation and gains from it? ... Astute.

gre.s: The investor proved remarkably ____: while others panicked and sold, she quietly bought shares she knew were undervalued and tripled her money within a year.
gre.clue: while others panicked and sold

example: An astute coach, Rahima noticed that the opposing bowler tired after five overs and told her batters to wait him out.

en: Bold and shameless, without any embarrassment
hook: BRAZEN: hard and shiny like BRASS, shameless.
story: Brazen. Bold and shameless, without any embarrassment. In the middle of a crowded bazaar in Sylhet, a man walked up to a vegetable stall, picked up three cauliflowers, and strolled away without paying, whistling. When the seller shouted, he turned around and waved. The seller [gasp] simply stared. Rifat, buying onions nearby, could hardly believe how brazen the man was. Brazen once meant made of brass: picture a face as hard and shiny as brass, unable to blush. So, what word describes someone boldly shameless? ... Brazen.

gre.s: Rather than hiding the forgery, the art dealer made a ____ attempt to sell it at the very gallery that owned the original.
gre.clue: Rather than hiding the forgery

example: In a brazen lie, the company called its river clean on the same day reporters filmed dead fish beside its outlet pipe.

en: Abundant; existing in large amounts
hook: COPIOUS: so many COPIES that there's plenty for all.
story: Copious. Abundant; existing in large amounts. During his first Eid at his in-laws' house in Chattogram, Mizan learned what hospitality means. Plates of mezban beef, polao, shemai and three kinds of pitha kept arriving, and every time he emptied his plate, someone filled it again. By evening he begged for mercy, smiling. The food had been copious, and so was the love behind it. Copious comes from the Latin copia, plenty, which you also hear in cornucopia, the horn of plenty. So, what word describes something in very large amounts? ... Copious.

gre.s: Far from being sparse, the explorer's journals are ____, documenting every plant, river, and conversation she encountered.
gre.clue: Far from being sparse

example: Copious rain in July filled the reservoirs around Rangamati, ending weeks of fear about a water shortage.

en: Warm, friendly, and polite
hook: CORDIAL: from the HEART (cor, as in cardiac).
story: Cordial. Warm, friendly and polite. When Tamanna moved into a new flat in Uttara, she was nervous about her neighbours. On the first evening, the woman next door knocked with a plate of hot shingara and a smile. "If you need anything, just ring." The building's guard learned her name the same day. Everyone was so cordial that Tamanna felt at home within a week. Cordial comes from the Latin cor, heart, the same root as courage: cordial greetings come from the heart. So, what word describes warm, friendly and polite behaviour? ... Cordial.

gre.s: Though the negotiations were tense, relations between the two delegations remained ____, and each side thanked the other warmly at the close.
gre.clue: each side thanked the other warmly

example: Although the two former partners rarely agreed on business, their emails stayed cordial, always ending with good wishes for each other's families.

en: Pretending to be shy; reluctant to give details
hook: COY: playing it COOL and shy.
story: Coy. Pretending to be shy; also, reluctant to give details. When the aunties at a wedding asked Rumi whether she had someone special in her life, she smiled, looked down at her bangles, and said, "Who knows?" Everyone saw her glance across the room at a young man in a blue panjabi. Her cousins [laugh] nudged each other. She was being coy. Coy comes from an old French word for quiet, the same root as quiet itself: a coy person goes quiet on purpose. So, what word describes someone pretending to be shy or holding back details? ... Coy.

gre.s: The minister was uncharacteristically ____ about her plans, deflecting every question about the coming election with a smile and a vague remark about the weather.
gre.clue: deflecting every question

example: The author was coy about the ending of her next novel, saying only that readers should keep some tissues nearby.

en: To distribute; to provide (a service)
hook: DISPENSE: like a water DISPENSER giving out water.
story: Dispense. To give out to many people; also, to provide a service. At a rural health clinic in Netrokona, nurse Fatema starts work at eight. She checks each prescription, then dispenses tablets, syrup and oral saline to a long line of patients, explaining every dose slowly. She also dispenses something free: patience. Mothers trust her more than anyone in the union. Think of a water dispenser in an office, giving out cups of water one by one: to dispense is to hand things out. So, what verb means to give out or distribute? ... Dispense.

gre.s: Rather than stockpile the scarce grain, the village council chose to ____ it equally among all households, giving each family the same small ration.
gre.clue: giving each family the same small ration

example: Machines on every platform of the new metro dispense single-journey cards in less than ten seconds.

en: A person who opposes official policy, especially of an authoritarian state
hook: DIS-SIDE-ent: on the other SIDE.
story: Dissident. A person who opposes official policy, especially in a harsh, controlling state. In the nineteen sixties, under military rule in Pakistan, Sadman's grandfather was a young poet in Dhaka who wrote verses criticising the government. He was arrested twice and his poems were banned, but students copied them by hand and passed them around. He was a dissident, and he never stopped writing. Dissident comes from the Latin for sitting apart: a dissident sits apart from those in power. So, what word names someone who openly opposes an authoritarian government? ... Dissident.

gre.s: The regime claimed to tolerate free speech, yet any ____ who criticized its policies in print could expect to be imprisoned or forced into exile.
gre.clue: who criticized its policies in print

example: After years in exile, the dissident novelist returned home to find her books finally sold openly in the capital's shops.

en: Outstandingly bad; shocking
hook: EGREGIOUS: so bad it stands out from the herd (e-greg = out of the flock).
story: Egregious. Outstandingly bad; shocking. When Jannat's university published its final exam results, every student in her class had the same mark: forty-two. Even the students who had been absent. Someone had copied one number down the whole column. Students crowded the notice board in disbelief, and the registrar quickly apologised for such an egregious error. Egregious comes from the Latin for out of the flock, the same root as gregarious: an egregious mistake stands out from the herd. So, what word describes a mistake so bad it is shocking? ... Egregious.

gre.s: The auditors uncovered an ____ error in the accounts, a miscalculation so large that it had inflated profits by millions.
gre.clue: so large that it had inflated profits by millions

example: Attributing a famous quotation to the wrong president was an egregious slip for a history professor writing in a national newspaper.

en: Puzzling and mysterious; hard to explain or read
hook: ENIGMA = a riddle. ENIGMATIC = like a riddle.
story: Enigmatic. Mysterious and hard to understand or read. Every afternoon, an old man in a grey shawl sat on the same bench in Ramna Park, feeding pigeons and writing in a small notebook. He never spoke to anyone. Some said he was a retired judge; others said a poet. Nusaiba, who jogged past daily, grew curious. One day he looked up, gave her an enigmatic smile, and went back to writing. An enigma is a riddle, so an enigmatic person is a living riddle. So, what word describes someone mysterious and hard to read? ... Enigmatic.

gre.s: Scholars still debate the meaning of the poem's ____ final line, which seems to contradict everything that came before it.
gre.clue: Scholars still debate the meaning

example: The only clue was an enigmatic chalk symbol on the warehouse door, unlike anything the detectives had seen before.

en: Making one feel very happy, excited, and energized
hook: EXHILARATING: EX-HILARIOUS, full of joy.
story: Exhilarating. Making you feel very happy, excited and full of energy. On her first speedboat ride across the Padma, Arpita stood at the front, wind whipping her hair, spray cooling her face, the river glittering in the sun. When the boat leapt over a wave, she [gasp] grabbed the rail, then [laugh] shouted with joy. It was the most exhilarating ten minutes of her year. Exhilarating shares a root with hilarious, from the Latin for cheerful: exhilarating moments fill you with bright joy. So, what word describes an experience that leaves you thrilled and full of energy? ... Exhilarating.

gre.s: For the young climbers, reaching the summit was ____, a moment of pure joy after weeks of exhausting effort.
gre.clue: a moment of pure joy

example: Watching Bangladesh chase down a huge total in the final over was exhilarating for the packed crowd at Mirpur.

en: Often changing one's mind, likes, or loyalties
hook: FICKLE: FLICKERS like a candle.
story: Fickle. Often changing your mind, likes or loyalties. In January, Ferdous told everyone at the tea stall that he supported Argentina. By the World Cup quarter-finals, he was wearing a Brazil jersey. After Brazil lost, he appeared in a German cap. His friends [laugh] started calling him the weather vane, turning with every wind. Ferdous is a fickle fan, and he knows it. Fickle sounds like flicker: picture a candle flame flickering this way and that, never steady. So, what word describes someone whose loyalty keeps changing? ... Fickle.

gre.s: Politicians who rely on the ____ support of voters soon learn that a single unpopular decision can turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents.
gre.clue: turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents

example: Mountain weather is fickle, so the guide packed rain jackets even though the morning sky was perfectly clear.

en: Not literal; using figures of speech like metaphors
hook: FIGURATIVE: a FIGURE of speech.
story: Figurative. Not literal; using figures of speech such as metaphors. When Sinthia's grandmother said, "My heart broke into a hundred pieces when you left for Australia," Sinthia's little brother looked worried and asked if she needed a doctor. Sinthia [chuckle] hugged him and explained that Nani was speaking in a figurative way. Her heart was fine; she simply missed Sinthia very much. Figurative comes from figure, as in a figure of speech: words that paint a picture rather than state a fact. Its opposite is literal. So, what word describes language not meant literally? ... Figurative.

gre.s: Readers who interpret the poet's 'burning city' as an actual fire miss the point; the phrase is ____, describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze.
gre.clue: describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze

example: Learners of English often stumble over figurative expressions such as 'break the ice', reading them word by word.

en: New and inexperienced; a young bird just learning to fly
hook: FLEDGLING: a baby bird just getting its feathers.
story: Fledgling. New and inexperienced; also, a young bird just learning to fly. On their balcony in Rajshahi, Rabbi watched a baby myna hop to the edge of its nest, flap hard, and drop clumsily onto the railing. A day later it was flying short circles over the lane. That same month, Rabbi started a fledgling business selling mangoes online, with three customers and a borrowed phone. To fledge is to grow the feathers you need to fly, so a fledgling is just getting its wings. So, what word describes something new and still learning to fly? ... Fledgling.

gre.s: Like many ____ enterprises, the start-up struggled during its first year, lacking both the experience and the capital that established competitors enjoyed.
gre.clue: lacking both the experience and the capital that established competitors enjoyed

example: The fledgling theatre company in Rajshahi staged its first play in a school hall, with borrowed costumes and folding chairs.

en: Filled with something undesirable; causing anxiety
hook: FRAUGHT: FREIGHT-loaded with danger.
story: Fraught. Filled with something unwanted, such as danger or worry. For the whole month that Mahfuz's family waited to hear whether their visas to join his father in Italy would be approved, the house was fraught with tension. His mother cooked without speaking, his grandmother prayed longer than usual, and every phone call made them jump. Fraught means loaded, and it shares an old root with freight: a fraught situation is loaded with trouble, like a ship heavy with cargo. It usually comes with with: fraught with danger. So, what word describes a situation loaded with worry? ... Fraught.

gre.s: The negotiations were ____ with danger from the start: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war that had only just ended.
gre.clue: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war

example: Moving their parents to Dhaka was a decision fraught with guilt for the siblings, who had once promised never to leave the village.

en: Quick to believe things, and so easily fooled
hook: GULLIBLE: like a sea GULL that swallows anything thrown at it.
story: Gullible. Quick to believe things, and so easily fooled. Upoma's uncle received a message saying he had won a lottery in London. All he had to do was send ten thousand taka for processing fees. He was on his way to the mobile banking shop when Upoma [gasp] grabbed his phone. "Mama, you never bought a ticket!" Her uncle laughed nervously. He was kind, but gullible. Picture a seagull swallowing anything thrown into the water: a gullible person swallows any story. So, what word describes someone easily fooled? ... Gullible.

gre.s: Far from being ____, the investigator questioned every claim the witness made, insisting on documents for even the most trivial details.
gre.clue: questioned every claim the witness made

example: Fake websites selling cheap concert tickets target gullible teenagers, who often discover the fraud only at the stadium gate.

en: To stir people up to violence or law-breaking
hook: INCITE: light a fire INSIDE the crowd.
story: Incite. To stir people up to violence or law-breaking. After a minor car accident on a highway near Gazipur, a crowd gathered. One man began shouting false claims that the driver had done it on purpose, urging people to smash the car. Shahin, a schoolteacher, stepped between them and calmly asked everyone to look at the facts. The crowd cooled, and the man who had tried to incite them slipped away. Incite shares a root with excite: to incite a crowd is to excite it toward harm. So, what verb means to stir people up to violence? ... Incite.

gre.s: Prosecutors argued that the pamphlets were written not merely to criticize the government but to ____ riots, pointing to passages that urged readers to burn public buildings.
gre.clue: urged readers to burn public buildings

example: The club banned a group of supporters for using social media to incite fights with rival fans after matches.

en: To put someone or something in danger
hook: JEOPARDIZE: put it in JEOPARDY.
story: Jeopardize. To put someone or something in danger. Labiba had a scholarship offer from a university in Canada, but she still needed to finish her final project. Two weeks before the deadline, her friends invited her on a long trip to Cox's Bazar. She thought it over and stayed home. Missing the deadline would jeopardize everything she had worked for. Jeopardize comes from jeopardy, from an old French phrase for a divided game, where the result could go either way. So, what verb means to put something at risk? ... Jeopardize.

gre.s: Officials warned that any further delay would ____ the entire bridge project, since the foreign loan would be withdrawn if construction had not begun by March.
gre.clue: since the foreign loan would be withdrawn

example: Leaking the exam questions could jeopardize the careers of every teacher at the school, even those who knew nothing about it.

en: To hate something or someone very strongly
hook: LOATHE: 'LOW-THE' — so low in your opinion that you hate it.
story: Loathe. To hate something very strongly. Topu loathes the traffic jam at Mohakhali. Every morning his bus sits there for an hour while horns scream and the air turns grey. He checks the time again and again and [sigh] counts the minutes he will never get back. Do not confuse loathe with loath, without the e, which means unwilling: Topu is loath to leave home any earlier, but he truly loathes the traffic. So, what verb means to hate something intensely? ... Loathe.

gre.s: Though he came to ____ the city's noise and crowds, the poet found he could not write anywhere else.
gre.clue: Though he came to

example: Most cats loathe water, which is why bathing them usually ends with scratched arms and a soaked bathroom floor.

en: To intervene to help resolve a dispute
hook: MEDIATE: stand in the MIDDLE.
story: Mediate. To step in and help settle a dispute. Two neighbours in Mithun's village had argued for months about a goat that kept eating the other's vegetables. Shouting turned to threats. Then the village schoolmaster invited both men to his veranda for tea. He listened to each side and suggested a bamboo fence paid for by both. Soon the two [chuckle] were arguing only about who would bring the bamboo. He had mediated the quarrel. Mediate comes from the Latin for middle: a mediator stands in the middle. So, what verb means to help two sides settle a dispute? ... Mediate.

gre.s: Because neither side trusted the other enough to negotiate directly, both agreed to let a neutral diplomat ____ the dispute over the contested border.
gre.clue: neither side trusted the other enough to negotiate directly

example: A retired judge was asked to mediate between the garment workers' union and the factory owners after wage talks collapsed.

en: Not literal; using one thing to represent another
hook: METAPHORICAL: uses a METAPHOR.
story: Metaphorical. Not literal; using one thing to stand for another. When Antara's teacher said that the Padma Bridge was a golden thread tying the country together, a boy in the front row asked whether it was really made of gold. Antara explained that the teacher was being metaphorical. The bridge is concrete and steel; the golden thread meant how it joins the southwest to the rest of the nation. Metaphor comes from the Greek for carry across: metaphorical words carry meaning from one thing to another. So, what word describes language that uses one thing to represent another? ... Metaphorical.

gre.s: When the poet describes the city as a cage, she is speaking in ____ terms, not complaining about any actual bars.
gre.clue: not complaining about any actual bars

example: The shattered mirror in the film's last scene is metaphorical, standing for the family that has broken apart.

en: To cancel out the effect of something, making it harmless
hook: NEUTRALIZE: make NEUTRAL, neither acid nor base.
story: Neutralize. To cancel the effect of something and make it harmless. After a plate of fuchka with extra tamarind water, Rajib's stomach burned all evening. His mother handed him an antacid tablet, and within minutes the burning eased: the tablet had neutralized the acid. In chemistry class the next day, his teacher showed how a base neutralizes an acid until the mixture is neither. Neutralize simply means to make neutral, taking neither side. So, what verb means to cancel out the effect of something? ... Neutralize.

gre.s: Her rivals hoped the scandal would sink the senator's campaign, but her swift and candid apology served to ____ its effects almost entirely.
gre.clue: swift and candid apology

example: Farmers add lime to their fields to neutralize soil that has grown too acidic after years of heavy fertiliser use.

en: To repeat something already said, usually to stress it
hook: RE-ITERATE: say it again and again (iterate).
story: Reiterate. To repeat something already said, usually to stress it. Before a field trip into the Sundarbans, the forest guide gathered Nabil's class on the boat. "Stay with the group. Do not touch the water. Do not wander into the forest." Then, as the boat docked, he reiterated every rule, more slowly. When they spotted a fresh tiger pawprint in the mud, [gasp] nobody needed the rules reiterated a third time. Iterate means to repeat, and re means again: to reiterate is to say it again, for emphasis. So, what verb means to repeat something to stress it? ... Reiterate.

gre.s: Because so many students had ignored the first notice, the principal felt obliged to ____ the warning in a second, more strongly worded letter.
gre.clue: Because so many students had ignored the first notice

example: At the press conference, the captain reiterated that he would retire after the World Cup, ending weeks of rumours.

en: To voluntarily give up or let go
hook: RELINQUISH: RELease and finISH.
story: Relinquish. To voluntarily give up or let go. For thirty years, Sraboni's grandfather ran the family sweet shop in Tangail, famous for its chomchom. At seventy-five, he finally handed the keys to his granddaughter. His hands shook as he gave them over, but he [sigh] smiled. Relinquishing the shop was hard, yet he knew it was time. Relinquish shares its Latin root with relic: both are about something left behind. To relinquish is to leave something behind willingly. So, what verb means to give up something willingly? ... Relinquish.

gre.s: The aging dictator refused to ____ power, even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin.
gre.clue: even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin

example: The champion boxer chose to relinquish his title rather than fight an opponent he believed had been doping.

en: Firmly decided and refusing to be turned aside
hook: RESOLUTE: full of RESOLVE.
story: Resolute. Firmly determined, refusing to be turned aside. When Imon decided to become the first woman in her village to study engineering, relatives told her it was impossible, and her uncle said girls should marry early. She ignored them, woke at five every morning to study, and walked an hour to the coaching centre. When she won a seat at a top engineering university, the same uncle brought sweets for the whole village. She had been resolute. Resolute comes from resolve: a resolute person makes a firm decision and keeps it. So, what word describes someone firmly determined? ... Resolute.

gre.s: Despite years of threats and imprisonment, the activist remained ____ in her demands for reform, refusing every offer of compromise from the government.
gre.clue: refusing every offer of compromise from the government

example: Resolute in her plan to swim the English Channel, Shabnam trained every dawn in the choppy sea off Cox's Bazar.

en: To strike back in response to an attack or insult
hook: RETALIATE: return the TALLY, an eye for an eye.
story: Retaliate. To strike back after an attack or insult. In a lane cricket match in Old Dhaka, Sagor bowled a tennis-ball bouncer that knocked off his friend's cap. The very next over, his friend grabbed the ball and bowled one straight back at Sagor's head. The other boys [laugh] shouted, "Revenge!" His friend had retaliated. Retaliate comes from the old Roman idea of talio, paying back like for like, the law of an eye for an eye. When someone hits you and you hit back, you retaliate. So, what verb means to strike back after being attacked? ... Retaliate.

gre.s: Fearing that the rival nation would ____ with punishing tariffs of its own, the government hesitated to impose new taxes on imported goods.
gre.clue: with punishing tariffs of its own

example: When the neighbour's goat ate her spinach for the third time, Nanu retaliated by planting chillies all along the fence.

en: Hardly enough; only a small amount
hook: SCANT: SCANTY, hardly enough.
story: Scant. Hardly enough; only a small amount. In the last week before payday, Mehreen's family lived on scant supplies: a little rice, a few potatoes and one bottle of oil. Her mother made every meal stretch, frying the potato peels until they were crisp. Nobody complained. Scant can also describe attention or evidence: a report with scant proof has barely any. Scant is the root of scanty, and it is the opposite of copious. So, what word means hardly enough? ... Scant.

gre.s: The theory has attracted wide popular attention despite ____ evidence, resting on a single study that has never been replicated.
gre.clue: resting on a single study that has never been replicated

example: The rescue team had scant information about the missing hikers, knowing only which valley they had entered.

en: Strong contempt; to reject with contempt
hook: SCORN: SCORE zero on respect.
story: Scorn. Strong contempt; to reject with contempt. When Bulbul said he wanted to quit his bank job and become a potter, his cousins treated the idea with scorn. "Playing with mud at your age?" Bulbul did not argue. He bought a wheel and worked every evening. Five years later, his clay pots sold in shops across Dhaka, and the same cousins asked him for discounts. Scorn sounds a little like score zero: when you scorn someone, you give them zero respect. So, what word names a strong feeling of contempt? ... Scorn.

gre.s: Purists tend to ____ any adaptation of a classic novel, dismissing even the most faithful film versions as cheap imitations.
gre.clue: dismissing even the most faithful film versions as cheap imitations

example: The veteran critic poured scorn on the sequel, calling it a lazy copy stitched together from leftover scenes.

en: Showing sharp judgment, especially in practical matters
hook: SHREWD: sharp as a SHREW's teeth.
story: Shrewd. Showing sharp judgment, especially in practical matters. At the Gabtoli cattle market before Eid, Tamal's grandfather walked slowly between the cows, checking teeth, eyes and legs. One seller demanded a high price. The old man shrugged, walked away, and returned an hour later, when it was getting dark and the seller was nervous. He bought the best cow for far less. He was shrewd. Shrewd grew from shrew, the tiny sharp-nosed animal: picture its sharp little eyes missing nothing. So, what word describes someone with sharp, practical judgment? ... Shrewd.

gre.s: A ____ investor, she sold her shares months before the crash, having recognized warning signs that most analysts had dismissed as insignificant.
gre.clue: having recognized warning signs that most analysts had dismissed

example: A shrewd judge of character, the old headmaster could tell within a minute whether a new teacher would last the year.

en: To go beyond the limits of
hook: TRANS-CEND: climb (scend) ACROSS (trans) the limits.
story: Transcend. To go beyond the limits of something. Shreya, a student from Kolkata, and Fahad, from Dhaka, met at a music evening in London. When the singer began a Tagore song, both of them sang along, word for word, and then looked at each other in surprise. Tagore wrote the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh, and his songs transcend borders. Trans means across, and scend means climb, as in ascend: to transcend is to climb across a limit. So, what verb means to go beyond the limits of something? ... Transcend.

gre.s: The finest translations ____ the limits of a word-for-word rendering; rather than merely copying sentences, they recreate the spirit of the original.
gre.clue: rather than merely copying sentences

example: Great children's books transcend their intended age group, delighting grandparents as much as the grandchildren they read to.

en: Quietly simple and tasteful rather than showy
hook: UNDER-STATED: stated less loudly than it could be.
story: Understated. Quietly simple and tasteful rather than showy. At a wedding full of glittering lehengas and heavy gold, Mehjabin wore a plain cream Jamdani sari, small pearl earrings, and a single white flower in her hair. Yet by the end of the night, every aunty had asked where she bought the sari. Her style was understated, quiet but impossible to forget. Understated means stated below its full volume: an understated look whispers instead of shouting. So, what word describes style that is simple and tasteful, not showy? ... Understated.

gre.s: Unlike the flashy designs of her rivals, the architect's ____ buildings blend quietly into their surroundings.
gre.clue: blend quietly into their surroundings

example: The actor's understated performance, built almost entirely from glances and silences, moved audiences more than any tearful speech.
